Abstract 25

26

Cybergenetic systems use computer interfaces to enable feed-back controls over 27

biological processes in real time. The complex and dynamic nature of cellular 28

metabolism makes cybergenetics attractive for controlling engineered metabolic 29

pathways in microbial fermentations. Cybergenetics would not only create new avenues 30

of research into cellular metabolism, it would also enable unprecedented strategies for 31

pathway optimization and bioreactor operation and automation. Implementation of 32

metabolic cybergenetics, however, will require new capabilities from actuators, 33

biosensors, and control algorithms. The recent application of optogenetics in metabolic 34

engineering, the expanding role of genetically encoded biosensors in strain development, 35

and continued progress in control algorithms for biological processes raise the prospect 36

that this technology will become available in the not so distant future. 37

Introduction 48

49

Cybergenetics is an emerging field that employs computer interfaces to control dynamic 50

biological processes in real-time by monitoring key parameters and using feed-back 51

controls to establish specific objectives [1–5]. Recent advances in optogenetic modulators, 52

genetically encoded biosensors, and control algorithms for cellular processes have 53

prepared the field of metabolic engineering for the imminent application of cybergenetics. 54

Using cybergenetic approaches to study or engineer cellular metabolism would expand the 55

capabilities of basic research and biotechnology and help to develop new modalities of 56

dynamic control for chemical production in microbial fermentations [6]. The systems we 57

envision comprise a strain engineered with a biosynthetic pathway for chemical production 58

and the three following cybergenetic elements: 1) genetically encoded optogenetic 59

actuators that enable the control of engineered and/or endogenous metabolic pathways with 60

light; 2) genetically encoded biosensors that report on the activity of the engineered 61

pathway and/or the metabolic state of the cell; and 3) computer algorithms that integrate 62

biosensor outputs to inform actuator inputs in closed-loop control systems to optimize 63

chemical production (Figure 1). 64

65

Most cybergenetic demonstrations have been conducted in microfluidic devices or in small 66

chemostat bioreactors suitable to study dynamic transitions between alternative steady or 67

semi-steady states (e.g., tracking a time-varying ramp or sinusoidal reference function) [7– 68

10]. Therefore, applying metabolic cybergenetics to the long non-continuous batch or semi- 69

batch fermentations typically used for microbial chemical production will require new 70

4

capabilities. In non-continuous experiments, actuators and biosensors must not only be 71

reversible, but also have response rates (of activation and inactivation) fast enough to 72

accurately induce effects and emit monitoring signals, respectively, within the timescales 73

of the required metabolic shifts. Equally crucial is that the actuators and biosensors are 74

functional throughout the fermentation despite changing conditions (e.g., growth phase, 75

substrate and product concentrations, cell density, etc.). Finally, control algorithms must 76

be able to handle inevitable delays and potential shifts during fermentations in the 77

correlations between actuators and their triggered responses, or biosensors and their 78

monitored parameters. Although many of these capabilities are not yet available and critical 79

obstacles still need to be overcome, especially for industrial scale applications, the variety 80

of existing optogenetic actuators, biosensors, and control algorithms for biological 81

processes [3,7,11–14] gives us reason to believe that metabolic cybergenetics for microbial 82

chemical production is on the horizon. 83

The Actuators 85

86

Optogenetic modulators are in many ways ideal actuators for metabolic cybergenetics in 87

non-continuous fermentations [11,15,16]. In contrast to the chemical inducers previously 88

used in cybergenetics [2,3,17], light can be instantly applied or removed to control batch 89

or semi-batch fermentations [18]. Optogenetic actuators are also advantageous in the face 90

of changing conditions as light inputs are reversible, highly tunable, operate independently 91

of media composition, and can induce highly specific outcomes with minimal cellular side- 92

effects [14,18–21]. Moreover, optogenetic systems can respond to a broad range of 93


<!-- Page 5 -->


5

wavelengths (from infrared to ultraviolet, Figure 2A), and can operate at the transcriptional, 94

post-transcriptional, or post-translational levels (Figure 2B-D). Optogenetic systems, 95

therefore, offer many opportunities to develop rapid and reversible actuators for use in 96

metabolic cybergenetics. 97

98

Optogenetic transcriptional controls respond to several wavelengths through varied 99

molecular mechanisms [15,22] (see optobase.org). Their activation spectra span from UV 100

to far red wavelengths [23] with distinct maximum excitation peaks (Figure 2A), although 101

there is often overlap between the blue and red bandwidths (from 430 to 660 nm). In 102

general, these regulators operate in either single- or two-component systems (Figure 2B), 103

both of which have been employed in cybergenetic applications. For example, a single 104

component system derived from the bacterial blue light-responsive transcription factor 105

EL222 was used to establish a feed-back control system to study real-time gene 106

transcription in single cells [20]. Separately, a transcription factor derived from light- 107

triggered CRY2/CIB1 heterodimerization enabled the development of a closed-loop 108

optogenetic compensation (CLOC) system which was employed to study feedback 109

regulation and the yeast pheromone response [24]. Additionally, the green and red light- 110

responsive CcaS-CcaR two-component system was used to develop closed-loop control of 111

GFP production and cellular growth rate in chemostats [9]. Some of these systems, in 112

addition to the blue-responsive pDawn circuit, have also been applied in metabolic 113

engineering for microbial chemical production [18,19] and metabolic flux studies [14,21]. 114

Furthermore, because they act at the transcriptional level, these regulators can also be 115

employed to develop optogenetic gene circuits [25–29], which can be used in metabolic 116

engineering [18,19]. These gene circuits expand the capabilities of optogenetic controls, 117

6

allowing them to regulate more complex processes [14,18,19,21]. For example, 118

optogenetic circuits such as the yeast OptoINVRT, can be used to invert the response to 119

light [18]. Although the versatility of transcriptional systems has made them the most 120

widely used in metabolic engineering and cybergenetics, their response rates are inherently 121

constrained by the rates of transcription and translation of the host organism. 122

123

By circumventing transcription, optogenetic systems that act at post-transcriptional level 124

have the potential to serve as faster actuators. The recent discovery of the bacterial LOV 125

photoreceptor PAL, which binds to short RNA aptamers preferentially in blue light, 126

enabled the development of optogenetic regulators of translation in bacteria and 127

mammalian cells [30]. A different strategy, called mRNA light-activated reversible 128

inhibition by assembled trap (mRNA-LARIAT), provides translational control by 129

sequestering mRNA in reversible blue light-assembled protein/RNA architectures. This 130

reduces mRNA access to ribosomes, thus decreasing protein synthesis [31] (Figure 2C). 131

While there are still relatively few optogenetic systems that operate post-transcriptionally, 132

the examples that do exist demonstrate the potential of adapting this approach for 133

cybergenetics. 134

135

Optogenetic systems that operate at the post-translational level bypass both transcription 136

and translation, thereby providing the fastest rates of response and reversibility. These 137

systems typically exploit light-triggered protein-protein interactions or the 138

masking/unmasking of degradation, subcellular localization (Figure 2D), or protease 139

cleavage sequences [11,15,16]. 140

They respond to a wide variety of wavelengths, from PhyB/PIF-derived systems 141

inactivated by infrared light to those derived from UVR8/COP1 systems activated by 142

ultraviolet light [32] (Figure 2A). Most systems, however, are derived from light-oxygen- 143

voltage (LOV) domains (including iLID-SspB, magnets, LINuS, LANS, LEXY, LINX, 144

and GLIMPSe) and therefore respond to blue light [11,15,16]. Additional blue-light 145

responsive systems include CRY2/CIB heterodimers, CRY2/CRY2 oligomers, and blue- 146

light dissociated PixELLs  [11,15,16]. 147

148

Post-translational optogenetic systems have enabled studies on complex dynamic systems. 149

PhyB/PIF and CRY2/CIBN have been utilized to investigate cell signaling [11], and both 150

iLID-SspB and CRY2/CIBN to study embryogenesis [33]. Additionally, light-controlled 151

assembly of synthetic liquid membraneless organelles, mediated by CRY2 (Figure 2D) or 152

PixELL systems, have been used to direct flux through branched metabolic pathways [34]. 153

Optical binders (OptoBNDRS) [35,36], chimeras of AsLOV2 and nanobodies or 154

monobodies (Figure 2D), which could be developed to reversibly bind any protein of 155

interest, may further expand the capabilities of this approach. These early demonstrations 156

suggest that cybergenetic systems may one day benefit from the fast-acting kinetics of post- 157

translational optogenetic actuators. 158

The variety of optogenetic systems available raises the possibility of combining multiple 160

actuators acting at different levels of control within a single strain. This would make it 161

possible to benefit from the different advantages that each level has to offer (Table 1); for 162

example, the rapid kinetics of post-translational controls with the robustness and economy 163

167

The ability to combine multiple optogenetic actuators responding to orthogonal inputs can 168

also be useful for metabolic cybergenetics. To optimize chemical production, it is often 169

necessary to balance the activity levels of enzymes in the biosynthetic pathway of interest 170

and essential competing pathways. Therefore, having multiple actuators to independently 171

control different sets of enzymes or pathways throughout non-continuous fermentations 172

would significantly increase the capabilities of cybergenetic systems and the complexity 173

of metabolic networks under control. The red/IR-responsive PhyB/PIF and UV receptors 174

UVR8/COP1, have been combined to orthogonally control signaling pathways in 175

mammalian cells [41]. Similarly, the phytochrome-based tools Cph1 (red/far red) and 176

CcaS-CcaR (green/red) have been employed orthogonally to demonstrate bicolor control 177

of gene expression [26,28]. Systems such as BpHP1/PpsR2 (far-red/red) and UirS-UirR 178

(violet/green), could also be integrated in multichromatic systems as their range of 179

activation wavelengths do not overlap with each other or with those of blue light-activated 180

systems (Figure 2A). Other pairs with overlapping activating wavelength spectra may still 181

be combined if at least one of them can be inactivated by a different non-overlapping 182

wavelength. For example, while activation of Phy/PIF is maximal in the red spectrum, it is 183

still sensitive to activation by blue light. However, because Phy/PIF is inactivated by IR, it 184

could still be orthogonally used with a blue light system, using both blue and IR 185

illumination to only activate the blue actuator. Overall, the diversity of optogenetic tools 186

The Biosensors 191

192

Genetically encoded biosensors have been widely applied in metabolic engineering, 193

enabling high throughput screens to identify better producing strains or hyperactive 194

enzyme mutants, and to optimize metabolic pathways [43]. Based on their mechanisms, 195

biosensors can be grouped into four major classes (Figure 3): 1) ligand-binding-protein- 196

fluorophore (LBPF) chimeras, including biosensors based on Förster (or fluorescence) 197

resonance energy transfer (FRET) and circularly permuted fluorescent proteins (CPFPs); 198

2) RNA aptamers; 3) transcription factors (TFs); and 4) G-protein coupled receptors 199

(GPCR). Each type of biosensor presents unique advantages and disadvantages (Table 1) 200

in their potential application to metabolic cybergenetics. 201

202

Biosensors based on LBPF chimeras are fusions of natural or engineered ligand binding 203

proteins and one or more fluorescent proteins (FPs). Conformational changes induced by 204

ligand binding or environmental conditions (e.g., pH or oxygen level) shift the fluorescence 205

profile of the chimera. In the case of FRET-based biosensors, the conformational change 206

modifies the orientation or distance between pairs of compatible FPs, which allows for the 207

transfer of energy from the excited reporter (donor) to its pair (acceptor), (Figure 3A) 208

[44,45]. The output of FRET biosensors is thus a ratio of emissions from the FP pair, which 209


<!-- Page 10 -->


10

reflects the intracellular ligand concentration. Although the dynamic range of FRET-based 210

biosensors is usually limited, in most cases less than 3-fold [46] , they can be relatively 211

easy to design if a binding protein for the target molecule is available. In CPFP-based 212

biosensors, ligand binding shifts the fused FP from an inactive to an active conformation 213

(Figure 3B) [45]. Therefore, the total fluorescence emitted by these biosensors is 214

proportional to the ligand concentration. The main advantage of LBPF chimera-based 215

biosensors for metabolic cybergenetics is their ability to toggle between activated and 216

inactivated states almost instantly. Several biosensors based on LBPF chimeras have been 217

used to monitor intermediate metabolites, such as pyruvate [47], cofactors like ATP [48] 218

(Figure 3B), and final products, such as the monoterpenoid ajmalicine [46] (Figure 3A). 219

Despite their high sensitivity and specificity, they require careful in vivo calibration as 220

intracellular variations can greatly modify their output [49], which could pose challenges 221

for their application in metabolic cybergenetics. 222

223

Biosensors based on RNA aptamers, short single stranded oligonucleotides, can sense 224

proteins, cofactors, metabolites, and other molecules with high affinity and specificity 225

[50,51]. Most commonly, these aptamers adopt alternative conformations, in which the 226

analyte-bound conformation creates a binding site for an exogenous fluorophore, which, 227

upon binding, emits a fluorescence signal [50]. A key advantage of these biosensors is that 228

aptamers for a wide variety of ligands can be obtained with the well-established in vitro 229

selection method SELEX [52]. These biosensors commonly attain nM to pM binding 230

affinities to specific molecules and have dynamic ranges of 2- to 20-fold [48,53]. Other 231

advantages of aptamers are their essentially instantaneous activation and their diminished 232


<!-- Page 11 -->


11

cross-talk with other ligands compared to protein-based sensors. However, their tight 233

binding is often practically irreversible, requiring aptamer degradation and fresh aptamer 234

transcription to attain signal reversibility, adding delays. Another disadvantage of these 235

biosensors is the need for fluorogenic additives, which can limit their use in large scale 236

fermentations. This class of biosensors has been used to monitor intracellular concentration 237

of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) [54] (Figure 3C), tetracycline, adenine [51], and to select 238

yeast strains with enhanced tyrosine production [53]. Despite their limitations, the 239

versatility of this class of biosensor holds enormous potential for metabolic cybergenetic 240

applications. 241

242

The biosensors most commonly used in metabolic engineering and synthetic biology are 243

based on ligand-dependent TFs [12,25,55]. These biosensors utilize transcriptional 244

regulators that respond to the direct binding of specific molecules, including final products, 245

precursors, or cofactors [56,57], to control the expression of a reporter (typically a FP, 246

*Figure 3D). Engineered variants with altered specificities can yield novel biosensors for 247*

different molecules [58–60]. Bacterial small-molecule binding transcription factors from 248

the lysR-type transcriptional regulator (LTTR) superfamily have been engineered to be 249

functional in yeast [61], greatly expanding the potential to develop biosensors for different 250

metabolites in eukaryotes. Many TF-based biosensors have been developed for metabolic 251

engineering applications [56,57], including for the production of fatty acid-derived 252

products (using the acyl-CoA-dependent bacterial TF FadR) [62], cis,cis-muconic acid 253

(CCM) (using the CCM-dependent LTTR BenM)[61,63], and branched-chain amino acid- 254

derived products (using the a-isopropylmalate-dependent fungal zinc-knuckle TF Leu3p) 255


<!-- Page 12 -->


12

(Figure 3D) [42]. Biosensors for metabolic states have also been developed, such as for the 256

NADH/NAD+ ratio using the redox-responsive bacterial Rex TF [64]. While TF-based 257

biosensors tend to have high dynamic ranges, the inevitable delays in their response and 258

reversibility caused by the transcription, translation, and degradation/dilution of reporters 259

raise concerns about their effectiveness in metabolic cybergenetics. Nevertheless, their 260

robustness and established impact in metabolic engineering make a strong case for 261

exploring their utility in this emerging field. 262

263

Biosensors based on GPCRs specialize in sensing specific extracellular molecules. They 264

typically exploit GPCRs heterologously expressed in yeast, designed to trigger its mating 265

signaling pathway to induce transcription of a reporter (usually a FP). For example, the 266

human MTNR1A and A2BR GPCRs have been employed to sense melatonin (Figure 3E) 267

and adenosine, respectively [65]. GPCRs have also been used to develop FRET-based 268

reporters, which have the potential to be used as biosensors for metabolic engineering and 269

cybergenetics (Figure 3F). It is expected that these biosensors would show enhanced 270

response and reversibility rates as they would circumvent reporter transcription, 271

translation, and degradation [66]. Key advantages of this class of biosensor include the 272

large and growing number of GPCRs identified for a broad range of chemicals and the 273

sensitivity obtained by signal cascade amplification. Additionally, they can be rationally 274

tuned and reprogrammed to monitor a variety of molecules [65]. While their reliance on 275

endogenous signaling pathways restricts their applicability in other host organisms, their 276

many advantages raise the prospects of using this class of biosensor for metabolic 277

cybergenetics in yeast. 278

The features that have made biosensors powerful tools for metabolic engineering are 280

unlikely to be sufficient for their successful implementation in metabolic cybergenetics.  In 281

addition to canonical considerations such as sensitivity, dynamic range, and maximum 282

output [65], biosensors applied to metabolic cybergenetics must also be reversible, show 283

fast activation/inactivation kinetics, and have the ability to accurately monitor analyte 284

concentrations throughout long non-continuous fermentations, including at high cell 285

densities where fluorescence quenching is a concern. However, advances in de-novo 286

biosensor design [67], novel biosensors to measure metabolites in real-time for pathway 287

optimization and monitoring [68], and the use of biosensors in combination with gene logic 288

circuits to control chemical production in real-time [58] foreshadow the feasibility of using 289

genetically encoded biosensors for metabolic cybergenetics. 290

The Controllers 292

293

Equally important to the success of metabolic cybergenetics is the implementation of 294

effective control algorithms. Cybergenetic studies have used different algorithms to 295

establish feedback controls over a range of biological processes. Proportional-integral 296

(PI) feedback control (which corrects set point deviations by measuring the current error 297

and its time integral) and model predictive control (MPC, which utilizes mathematical 298

models of the system to predict the output that will minimize the error over a time period) 299

have been used to control GFP expression and growth rate [3,9,10,24]. PI controllers 300

have the advantage of being relatively simple and not requiring a mathematical model of 301


<!-- Page 14 -->


14

the system. Additionally, they are effective at controlling systems with constant setpoints 302

and rejecting constant perturbations. They fail, however, to adequately control systems 303

with time-varying reference points or rejecting variable perturbations, for which MPC 304

algorithms are much more effective [9]. Although MPC algorithms require at least a 305

crude mathematical model of the system, they are superior for handling delays such as 306

those caused by transcription or translation [24]. 307

308

Other controllers have proven to be useful for cybergenetics. The ‘bang-bang’ controller, 309

which applies maximal or minimal control outputs depending on the sign of the deviation 310

from setpoint, and zero average dynamics (ZAD), an approach derived from sliding 311

control techniques, have been employed to control protein concentrations at fixed and 312

time-varying references [3,7].  The ‘bang-bang’ controller has also been used to maintain 313

a toggle switch in unstable equilibrium for extended periods of time, aided by a 314

deterministic model of pseudo-reactions representing reporter transcription, translation, 315

and degradation/dilution [69]. While a PI controller was able to maintain only a single 316

cell away from the stable states of the toggle switch, the “bang-bang” controller proved 317

effective at also maintaining multiple cells at unstable equilibrium. This was done using 318

periodic forcing [69], for which optogenetics is ideally suited [18]. 319

320

The ability of some of these algorithms (e.g., MPC and ‘bang-bang’) to track time-varying 321

references and reject dynamic perturbations makes them particularly attractive to control 322

complex dynamic systems. The recent development of an integral feedback controller that 323

rejects noise as well as external and internal perturbations for robust and perfect adaptation, 324


<!-- Page 15 -->


15

is another important step in the right direction [70]. Alternative approaches, in cases where 325

system delays are insurmountable, may use controls guided by neural networks trained 326

with limited data sets, enabled by “gray box” models that incorporate physical knowledge 327

of the system. This critical data may be acquired from high through-put experiments such 328

as those using 96-well optoPlates [71]. Although none of these algorithms have yet been 329

tested in large batch or semi-batch fermentations, their capabilities to efficiently and 330

accurately handle delays, varying references, and dynamic perturbations open the door to 331

their application in metabolic cybergenetics. 332

The Equipment: Closing the Loop 334

335

Key to realizing the goals of metabolic cybergenetics is the development of proper 336

equipment. Most cybergenetic demonstrations have been done in low-volume continuous 337

systems (e.g., microfluidic devices or small chemostats) [8–10,24] or relatively short- 338

lived experiments [72]. This facilitates the use of light stimuli or even chemical inducers 339

as inputs for actuators, given that volumes are small, there are no impediments to light 340

penetration, and flexible experimental time-lengths can be extended as necessary. 341

Implementing metabolic cybergenetics in bioreactors for microbial chemical production, 342

however, will require different infrastructure because of the high cell densities they 343

typically achieve and their non-continuous operation. 344

345

While fluorescence may be continuously monitored in bioreactors using commercial 346

probes [73] or sample streams for flow cytometry [9], using optogenetic actuators can be 347


<!-- Page 16 -->


16

problematic as light penetration in large fermentations will likely be limiting. 348

Fermentations at cell densities of up to at least 50 OD600 in bioreactors of up to at least 5 L 349

can be controlled with light by illuminating well-mixed cultures with LED panels through 350

the walls of a glass vessel [18] (Figure 4A). It is conceivable that a similar approach could 351

be employed in larger industrial transparent plastic bioreactors [74]. Alternatively, many 352

photobioreactors designed for photosynthetic organisms [75] could be repurposed, 353

including several with submerged LEDs (Figure 4B). Another possibility is recirculating 354

the fermentation broth through constantly illuminated transparent chambers, sometimes 355

used for photoactivation of chemical reactions, the flow rate of which would set the 356

frequency of forcing periods (Figure 4C). Despite the uncertainty of how metabolic 357

cybergenetics may be implemented in industrial settings, its feasibility in lab-scale 358

bioreactors is more predictable, which would open new research avenues in metabolic 359

dynamics to better understand and optimize metabolic pathways (Figure 4D). 360

Conclusion 362

363

Metabolic cybergenetics could transform the way we study metabolic dynamics, optimize 364

engineered pathways, or even design and operate bioreactors for microbial chemical 365

production. Although these strategies have tremendous potential, many challenges still lie 366

ahead before researchers can practically implement metabolic cybergenetic approaches. 367

These challenges include developing actuators and biosensors that are rapid, reversible, 368

and functional throughout long non-continuous fermentations, as well as control 369

algorithms that can handle inevitable delays and potential drifts in actuator/biosensor 370


<!-- Page 17 -->


17

correlations to their cellular functions. Overcoming light penetration limitations will also 371

be important for industrial applications. Nevertheless, the recent application of 372

optogenetics to metabolic engineering, the expanding capabilities of genetically encoded 373

biosensors, and ongoing efforts to develop controllers for increasingly complex 374

biological processes have set the stage for the coming of metabolic cybergenetics. 375

# Using MitER for 3D analysis of mitochondrial morphology and ER contacts

**Authors:** Therese Kichuk; Satyen Dhamankar; Saurabh Malani; William A. Hofstadter; Scott A. Wegner; Ileana M. Cristea; José L. Avalos

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Molecular Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA | 2Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA | 3The Andlinger Center for Energy and the Environment, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA | 4High Meadows Environmental Institute, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA | 5Omenn-Darling Bioengineering Institute, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA

## Abstract

We have developed an open-source workflow that allows for quantitative single-cell analysis of organelle morphology, distribution, and inter-organelle contacts with an emphasis on the analysis of mitochondria and mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum (mito-ER) contact sites. As the importance of inter-organelle contacts becomes more widely recognized, there is a concomitant increase in demand for tools to analyze subcellular architecture. Here, we describe a workflow we call MitER (pronounced “mightier”), which allows for automated calculation of organelle morphology, distribution, and inter-organelle contacts from 3D renderings by employing the animation software Blender. We then use MitER to quantify the variations in the mito-ER networks of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, revealing significantly more mito-ER contacts within respiring cells compared to fermenting cells. We then demonstrate how this workflow can be applied to mammalian systems and used to monitor mitochondrial dynamics and inter-organelle contact in time-lapse studies.

Mitochondrial morphology and contact with proximal organelles are important in both healthy and diseased cell states. Quantification of mitochondrial contact with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is particularly valuable as these contacts influence numerous cellular processes, such as mitochondrial fission and fusion, mitophagy, and calcium signaling. However, there are limited tools for such quantitative analyses. Current open-source methods solely allow for colocalization measurements, which are sufficient to estimate inter-organelle contact but lack the ability to provide more substantial metrics, such as the surface area and number of discrete contacts.

## Abstract

Kichuk et al. introduce MitER, an open-source workflow that allows for quantitative single-cell analysis of organelle morphology, distribution, and inter-organelle contacts. The workflow is used to quantify the variations in the mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum (mito-ER) networks of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, revealing a significant increase in mito-ER contacts within respiring cells compared to fermenting cells.

## Introduction

Mitochondria have long been known for their importance to normal cellular function. These organelles are responsible for cellular respiration, metabolism, and programmed cell death.1 Mitochondrial dysfunction and its associated morphological changes are common characteristics in numerous disease processes. Mitochondria, however, do not function independently of other organelles, and their behavior can be better understood through their interactions with other subcellular compartments. Mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum (mito-ER) contacts are increasingly recognized for their importance in fundamental cellular processes and to the pathophysiology underlying numerous diseases. These contacts are hubs for lipid transport, calcium signaling, and mitophagy. Moreover, disruptions in these contact sites are implicated in the pathophysiology of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and Parkinson’s disease.2,3

Recent studies of mito-ER contacts have been enabled by the visualization of mito-ER overlap in live cells with fluorescence microscopy.4 The availability of image analysis tools to analyze inter-organelle contact sites, however, lags behind the ability to collect high-quality imaging data. Open-source software like Fiji5 allows researchers to obtain colocalization measurements, but these measurements do not allow for meaningful characterization of mito-ER interactions. In mammalian cells, for example, 5%–20% of the mitochondrial surface is reported to be in contact with the ER,6 but little is known about the precise number of discrete contacts, or the surface area of each. Analysis of 3D electron tomography data has provided a more detailed picture of the size of these contacts,7 but acquiring these data can be challenging and the requirement to freeze the sample prohibits live-cell imaging.

In this study, we show how mitochondrial morphology and ER contacts in living yeast cells can be quantified in greater detail by using a 3D rendering-based approach to analyze fluorescence microscopy images. We leverage the open-source rendering software MitoGraph8 to obtain high-quality renderings of subcellular structures. Then, using the open-source animation software Blender,9 we measure various structural characteristics of these renderings. We automate this process in a workflow we call MitER that can be used to analyze microscopy images of live or fixed cells. Using standard confocal fluorescent images, MitER allows for the estimation of cell volume and surface area in addition to the determination of mitochondrial morphology and inter-organelle contact. Using MitER, we measure changes in mitochondrial surface area, mito-ER contacts, and mitochondrial distribution in Saccharomyces cerevisiae as cells switch from fermentation to respiration. Additionally, we employ MitER to investigate the dynamic behavior of these cells during this metabolic transition and demonstrate how this workflow can be applicable to mammalian systems. This method addresses the growing need for tools to analyze inter-organelle contacts, mitochondrial morphology, dynamics, and organelle localization.

### 3D segmentation allows for single-cell analysis of cell clusters

Although other rendering software can be used, we employed the open-source program MitoGraph to render both the mitochondrial and ER fluorescent signals within each cell (Figure 1C). By duplicating the defined region of interest (ROI) between channels, the resulting renderings preserve the spatial positioning of each organelle relative to one another. Because of the challenge of accurately defining 3D ROIs in Fiji, we opened the VTK files exported from MitoGraph in ParaView11 to further segment renderings of clusters containing between 2 and 3 cells. In this way, we ensured that downstream analysis would only be conducted on single cells regardless of whether or not the yeast was budding along the z-axis. This additional segmentation step allows us to select single cells along three axes, avoiding the need to resolve cells solely by a two-dimensional ROI. In this manner, 3D segmentation allows for more cells to be analyzed per image.

### Pre-processing in ParaView enables cell surface estimation from ER signal

Following 3D segmentation, the cell surface can be estimated by applying a Delaunay 3D filter to the ER mesh in ParaView. The output is a tetrahedral mesh approximating the outermost points of the ER rendering. Given that this organelle abuts the intracellular plasma membrane surface, this signal can serve as a proxy for the cell surface (Figure 1D). Estimation of the cell surface and the creation of this additional mesh allows for downstream analysis of three structures (ER, mitochondria, and cell surface) from only two fluorescent channels (ER and mitochondria). We found that the periphery of the ER signal is highly correlated to the cell surface during both fermentation and respiration. Cell volumes estimated by the ER signal are on average 85.4% of the volumes measured more accurately using a MemBrite cell-wall dye (approximately 85% and 86% for fermenting and respiring cells, respectively) (Figure S1). To account for this slight and consistent discrepancy, the MitER script scales the volume of the cell surface as estimated by the ER by 1.17× (calculated from the inverse of 0.854) to correct for the underestimation in cell volume. As a further quality control, we ensure that all cells used in downstream analysis contain 99% of their mitochondrial volume within the corrected cell perimeter. This excludes cells with very poor ER renderings such that the Delaunay 3D surface of these ER signals would not encapsulate the mitochondria.

The advantage of estimating the cell surface from the ER signal is that it eliminates the need for a dye, which avoids additional incubation steps that can interfere with cell physiology. This method also leaves an additional fluorescent channel available to mark other subcellular structures if needed. Once cells are segmented and the cell surface mesh is created, the scene containing the renderings of each subcellular component is exported as an .x3d file, which is compatible with the MitER workflow in Blender.

### Import into Blender and cell structure labeling

Although segmentation and pre-processing are manual, the remainder of the protocol is automated with minimal required user input. The program prompts the user to select the folder containing the .x3d files of each single-cell scene. These are then automatically imported and analyzed. Cell structures are detected and automatically labeled (Figure 1E). First, the program identifies the structure with the largest volume and recognizes it as the cell. Second, the ER is identified as the structure with the same bounding box (the smallest cuboid drawn around a set of points such that all the points are within that cuboid) dimensions as the cell surface but a smaller mesh volume. This labeling strategy is effective as the cell surface is computed from the ER surface and, therefore, both structures will share bounding box dimensions. The remaining structure is identified as the mitochondria. The automated workflow is also compatible with two structure systems where only the cell surface and a single additional organelle are marked. The structure with the smallest volume corresponds to the organelle in question whose asymmetry and distribution is analyzed based on the larger structure (assumed to be the cell surface).

### Obtaining measurements of cell components

A key benefit to using Blender for single-cell analysis is the ability to take advantage of native functions within the software for accurate surface area and volume measurements. Converting each organelle to a triangulated mesh object and correcting non-manifold geometries allows us to quickly and easily calculate the surface area and volume of each subcellular component (Figure 1F). More complicated cellular measurements such as Booleans used for computing intersections between objects (discussed below) can be aided by simplifying the mesh (by calling the Remesh modifier in Blender) and specifying a voxel size (here, we chose a voxel size of 0.03). At this voxel size, this operation preserves organelle volume and overall shape but simplifies the topology to improve downstream calculations using Boolean modifiers. In our study, each organelle surface mesh was made manifold, re-meshed using a voxel size of 0.03, and triangulated prior to volume and surface area measurements.

In addition to volume and surface area measurements, we can obtain information regarding the structure’s spatial dimensions by exporting bounding box vertices. The center of gravity of each mesh object in the scene is computed by assuming they have uniform density and finding the center of mass based on the volume. The number of individual mitochondria in addition to their volumes and surface areas are computed by splitting the mitochondrial channel by connected components such that each individual mitochondrion is identified as a separate object.

### Inter-organelle contact and organelle distribution

Blender also allows for the computation of object intersections. By applying the intersection Boolean modifier in Blender to the ER and mitochondria channels (which preserves only the overlapping components between these objects), we compute the number and volume of mito-ER contacts, and we determine the surface area of the contacts from the surface area of the overlap volumes (corrected by a factor of 0.5 so as to not double count the contact surface area) (Figures 1G and 2A). We also employ the intersection Boolean to quantify organelle distribution within the cell. To determine organelle distribution, we discretized the radial cumulative distribution function by scaling down the cell volume (making twenty concentric sections increasing by equal volumes while keeping the center the same) at various fractions between 0 and 1 (Figure 2B, left). We then used the resulting concentric shapes to section the cell, calling on the intersection Boolean function to compute the volume of the organelle of interest in each subsection. ### Analysis of cell measurements in R

The MitER pipeline outputs (1) organelle surface area, (2) organelle volume, (3) the volume of each inter-organelle contact, and (4) the surface area of the volume of each inter-organelle contact. Using a separate R script, we analyzed these raw data into useful metrics such as total contact count and the number of contacts above a user-defined volume cutoff. As mentioned above, the surface area of each contact site was derived in R by halving the surface area of the volume of the inter-organelle overlap with the assumption that the contact site has half of its surface abutting one organelle and the other half lining the other organelle. The organelle volume, the organelle surface area, and the inter-organellar surface area measurements in each subsection can be used to compute their subcellular distributions (Figure 2B).

MitER calculates both volume and surface area distributions to give the user options regarding their metric of interest. To calculate volume distributions, the organelle volume and contact volume in each subcellular subsection can be used directly as reported by Blender. To calculate surface area distributions, however, care must be taken to not include in the extra surface area created by the slicing of the organelle during cell subsectioning, as Blender interprets the sliced organelle as being a complete organelle. The true surface area of the organelle present in the section, S A o r g a n e l l e , is calculated with Equation 1.Equation (1) S A o r g a n e l l e = S A s e c t i o n + S A d i f f e r e n c e − S A s u r f a c e 2 , where S A s e c t i o n is the organelle surface area in the section reported by Blender, S A s u r f a c e is the surface area of the cell subsection, and S A d i f f e r e n c e is the resulting surface area when the organelle is subtracted from the sectioning shape (Figure 2C). The calculated distribution metrics can be used to describe complicated organelle characteristics such as situations in which there is predominantly central organelle volume, while the majority of the surface area is found toward the periphery of the cell.

The R script also computes the asymmetry in the organelle distribution by taking the Euclidean distance between the center of gravity of the cell and the center of gravity of the organelle components (Figure 2D). This is then normalized by the mean cell radius to yield a unitless number between 0 and 1, with 0 indicating perfect angular symmetry around the cellular center and 1 indicating maximal asymmetry.

### Comparison to current methods

To validate our approach, we compared our method against current gold-standard approaches. We compared the organelle volume measurements from the MitER workflow in Blender to the values obtained with MitoGraph and Imaris from the same renderings (Figures S2A and S2B). We found that our volume measurements agreed with those calculated by both MitoGraph and Imaris. Additionally, we compared the mitochondrial and ER surface area measurements calculated by MitER and Imaris (Figure S2C). Once again, we found complete agreement between the measurements reported by each method. As a final verification, we compared inter-organelle overlap volumes calculated by MitER with those reported by Imaris from the same renderings (Figure S2D). For any given yeast rendering, the outputs from MitER and Imaris are the same.

To validate the use of MitoGraph to estimate inter-organelle contacts, we compared MitER outputs using MitoGraph renderings to MitER outputs using Imaris renderings of the same cells (Figure S3). Specifically, we looked at the fraction of organelle volume (Figure S3A) accounted for by the volume of inter-organelle contact (contact volume/organelle volume). We then looked at the fraction of organelle surface area (Figure S3B) accounted for by the surface area of the overlap between the structures (contact surface area/organelle surface area). Using these measurements, we can find what fraction of the mitochondrial surface is in contact with the ER and vice versa. We found a strong correlation in the outputs between MitoGraph and Imaris renderings, confirming the validity of the open-source rendering method used in this study.

### MitER for mammalian cells

Although MitER is optimized to analyze yeast cells, many of the measurements also prove useful for mammalian cell analysis (Figure 6). Mammalian cells are more challenging to analyze than yeast cells. Their surfaces are far more irregular than the spheroid yeast cell morphology, and as the renderings of mammalian structures can be over 1 GB, running the workflow on files this large can be prohibitively slow. Nevertheless, the workflow can be adapted to provide useful measurements for mammalian systems. Prior to cell surface estimation, the mesh can be simplified using the Decimate modifier in Blender. This modifier simplifies the vertex count while preserving overall topology. With this strategy, prior to analysis, we reduced organelle renderings to 20% of their original size by setting the vertex ratio to 0.05. These smaller files could then be opened in ParaView for cell surface estimation. The estimation of cell surface area and volume by the ER signal still holds true in mammalian cells as the ER runs parallel to the mammalian plasma membrane.14 Therefore, the Delaunay triangulation protocol can be adapted to compute these more complicated cell shapes (Figure 6A). Even for highly complicated mammalian organelle networks, MitER and Imaris produce the same volume (Figure 6B) and surface area (Figure 6C) measurements. MitER can be adapted to provide measurements regarding organelle distribution in mammalian systems. As mammalian cell morphologies are far more complex than those found in yeast cells, simply scaling down the cell topology is not appropriate for sectioning the cell. To address this issue, we can again turn to the Remesh modifier in Blender, this time specifying a voxel size of 1 (as opposed to the voxel size of 0.03 used for Remeshing cellular components to aid with Boolean operations). By specifying a larger voxel size, we take advantage of the loss of topological detail and obtain an estimate of the mammalian cell body without the large protrusions most problematic for cell sectioning (Figure 6Ei). This simplified cell body estimate can then be duplicated, scaled down, and nested to obtain concentric volumes to section the cell (Figure 6Eii). The volumes of each resulting section are then compared to the total mammalian cell volume to determine the fraction of cell volume in each section, and the mitochondrial volumes in each resulting section are compared to the total cellular mitochondrial volume to determine the fraction of mitochondrial volume in each section (Figure 6F). Therefore, while MitER could be further optimized for mammalian cells, as it stands, it is very well suited to study inter-organelle contacts in mammalian systems.

### MitER for organelle dynamics

Single-cell measurements obtained with MitER can be particularly powerful in the context of time-lapse studies of organelle dynamics. Population-level data of these dynamic phenomena, while useful, can miss the finer shifts organelles undergo as they switch between metabolic states. We employed the MitER workflow to time-lapse data of yeast undergoing the transition from fermentation to respiration. Using MitER, it is possible to track changes in volume, surface area, and inter-organelle contacts in single cells across time. In this proof-of-concept experiment, we imaged yeast cells initially grown in glucose and then switched into media containing glycerol and ethanol as the sole carbon sources 1 h prior to imaging. We imaged the cells every 45 min for 12 h (Figure 7A). We then selected 6 cells from the population, rendered them in MitoGraph, and analyzed them with the MitER script in Blender. Using these data, we can make detailed analyses of mitochondrial dynamics, including changes in volume (Figure 7B), surface area (Figure 7C), and mito-ER contact surface area changes (Figure 7C) over time. Looking at cell A and cell B (Videos S1 and S2 respectively), we observe that both subtle (Cell A) and profound (Cell B) volume and surface area changes over time are captured by MitER analysis. ## Discussion

In this study, we developed an open-source image analysis pipeline for the quantification of the morphology and cellular distribution of mitochondria and mito-ER contacts. In constructing our workflow, we aimed to maximize the number of meaningful measurements we could obtain without the need for complicated sample preparation. Our pipeline allows for simple 3D segmentation and estimation of the cell surface from the ER fluorescent signal. To demonstrate the functionality and accuracy of our method, we analyzed single yeast cells in three different metabolic states.

Our pipeline produced measurements consistent with both previous studies and with peer-reviewed methods such as MitoGraph.8 We observed an increase in both mitochondrial volume and surface area in respiration relative to fermentation and an increased number of mito-ER contacts in respiration relative to both fermenting and transitioning cells. These findings indicate that mitochondria increase in surface area and volume prior to increasing contact with the ER. We also found that in all conditions, most of the mitochondrial volume exists in the periphery of the cell, but respiring cells exhibit a higher concentration of peripheral mitochondria compared to fermenting cells. Fermenting cells, on the other hand, display the most asymmetry in mitochondrial distribution. These differences in mitochondrial configurations could be crucial cellular adaptations to different metabolic states, and the mitochondrial morphological transitions observed in cells shifting from growing in glucose to growing in glycerol and ethanol are likely main contributors to the lag in growth as cells adapt to the new growth condition.

MitER can be used to screen large numbers of cells with minimal user input. Aside from cell segmentation and pre-processing, the workflow is entirely automated. Therefore, MitER is well suited to investigate disease processes that disrupt mitochondrial behavior such as dysfunctional mitophagy and altered fission and fusion processes. This workflow could also be used to characterize and design yeast mitochondria for optimal chemical production, as mitochondria are common targets of metabolic engineering for biosynthetic applications.15,16

MitER can serve as a powerful substitute for colocalization measurements to analyze the contacts between very small structures as it is only limited by the resolution of the microscope used for imaging. MitER is also well suited to analyze other inter-organelle contacts such as the peroxisome-ER interactions (Figure 6D), mitochondria-vacuole interactions, and organelle contact with the nucleus. Furthermore, the program allows for the measurement of discrete organelles when only one subcellular structure is marked in addition to the cell surface and when overlap measurements are of no interest.

In conclusion, freely available MitER has many of the commonly used capabilities found in costly commercial software that would help mitigate rising expenses in academic and industrial labs.17 This workflow addresses the growing need for open-source image analysis tools for organelle morphology and interactions and enables a better quantitative understanding of the complexity of the subcellular environment.

### Limitations of the study

As is the case with most imaging analysis techniques, the quality of the results depends on the quality of the imaging. If there is a substantial offset between fluorescent channels, both the colocalization and rendering results will be affected. Additionally, rendering-based approaches will not compensate for poor fluorophore expression. A strong fluorophore signal is a prerequisite to both reliable renderings and colocalization measurements.

In this pipeline, we use MitoGraph to produce our renderings due to its relative ease of use and it being an open-source program. MitoGraph, however, is sensitive to fluorophore signal intensity relative to the background, and poor signal can lead to an underestimation of the volume of a structure. On occasion, the software may not register any structure in the specified ROI. Some commercial programs have machine learning tools to compensate for low signal and to produce high-quality renderings, but commercial rendering software is often prohibitively expensive.

Manual 3D segmentation and application of the Delaunay 3D filter prevents this workflow from being completely automatic. The requirement that the user processes each cell individually is the bottleneck that limits the maximum number of cells that can be practically analyzed. However, this also provides the opportunity for quality control to ensure minimal background, acceptable structure rendering, and proper channel alignment. This step also allows for single cells to be precisely sectioned from renderings of cell clusters—an asset during live-cell imaging of budding yeast. Future efforts to automate the segmentation and filtering steps would enable the use of MitER in high-throughput applications, but it would be necessary to introduce quality control algorithms to maintain the same high-quality results.

### Experimental model and study participant details

#### Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain construction

The background strain used in this study is CEN.PK2-1C. To label the mitochondria, we expressed GFPmut3 fused on its N-terminus with the mitochondrial localization signal (the first 26 amino acids) of COX4. To label the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), we expressed mCherry fused on its N-terminus to an ER signal sequence (SS) and on its C-terminus to the HDEL ER retention signal.10 Constructs Cox4-GFPmut3 and pTPI1-SS-mCherry-HDEL (Addgene #133647) were linearized with pmeI and pacI, respectively, and integrated into the HIS3 and TRP1 genomic loci, respectively. Cox4-GFPmut3 is flanked by a TPI1 promoter and a CYC1 terminator (Figure S5). SS-mCherry-HDEL (Addgene #133647) is flanked by a TDH3 promoter and an ADH1 terminator. To further label Mmm1p, we integrated GFPmut3 following the endogenous Mmm1 along with HIS3 (Figure S6). Sequential strain transformations were done for each construct using the basic lithium acetate transformation protocol19 resulting in strain yTK32 (MATa; leu2-3_112; ura3-52; MAL2-8c; SUC10) marking mitochondria and ER and strain yTK55 (MATa; leu2-3_112; ura3-52; MAL2-8c; SUC10) marking Mmm1p and ER. Transformant colonies were selected on dropout media plates: synthetic complete (SC)-histidine or SC-tryptophan, as appropriate.

#### Mammalian strain construction

MRC-5 primary human lung fibroblast cells (ATCC CCL-171) were cultured at 37°C with 5% CO2 in media containing high glucose DMEM, 10% FBS, penicillin and streptomycin. To visualize organelles, fluorescent plasmids were transfected into cells. Mito-BFP (Addgene #49151) was used for visualization of mitochondria at 300 ng/mL, GFP-Sec61b (Addgene #15108) was used for visualization of the ER at 300 ng/mL. Transfections were carried out by first incubating our desired plasmids with 3 mL of X-tremeGENE HP DNA transfection reagent (Sigma-Aldrich) per 1 mg of DNA, diluted in Opti-MEM (Life Technologies). After 20 min at room temperature, the mixture was added dropwise to cells containing fresh warmed Opti-MEM. These cells were incubated at 37°C with 5% CO2 for 5.5 h prior to trypsinization and re-seeding into 35mm glass bottom microscope dishes (MatTek).

### Method details

#### Yeast culture and imaging

#### Single time point

Yeast cells were grown overnight in autoclaved and filtered synthetic complete (SC) media containing 2% glucose (Glu) and SC media containing 3% glycerol and 2% ethanol (GE). A single colony from a YPD plate containing yTK32 was inoculated into SC-Glu media and grown overnight in 24 well plates. In order to catch the cells during the mid-exponential phase, this overnight culture was inoculated into 1 mL SC-GE in 1:50, 1:100, and 1:500 dilutions. The overnight culture was inoculated into 1 mL SC-Glu in 1:500, 1:1000, 1:2000 dilutions. These cultures were set to grow overnight at 30°C in 24 well plates at 200 RPM. Once the cells reached mid-exponential phase (between OD600 = 4 and 5), cells were diluted 1:50 in 1 mL of either SC-Glu or SC-GE in a fresh 24-well plate. Cells that grew overnight in Glu medium were used to inoculate GE and Glu media whereas cells that grew overnight in GE medium were used to inoculate GE medium only. Following inoculation, cells were incubated at room temperature without shaking for 3 h and then adhered to 96-well plates pretreated with concanavalin A. To image cells, 96-well glass bottom plates (Cellvis, P96-1.5H-N) were pretreated for cell adhesion by pipetting 15 mL of 1 mg/mL concanavalin A (ConA) in 20 mM NaOAc and centrifuged for 1 min at 1,000 RPM. Plates were then incubated at room temperature for 1 h. Following incubation, wells were washed twice with 100 mL phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and allowed to dry for 1 h at room temperature, after removing most of the last wash volume. Once the wells were dry, 50 mL of the diluted cells (see above) were added to each well and the plate was centrifuged for 2 min at 1,000 RPM.

As cell stains sometimes interact with concanavalin A, yeast for studies involving dye were adhered using poly-L-lysine (Sigma). For these trials, the 96-well plate was pretreated with 50 μL of cold poly-L-Lysine and spun down for 1 min at 1000 RPM. After 5 min of incubation, the solution was removed by aspiration and washed twice with PBS. The treated wells were then allowed to dry for 2 h before introducing cells and media.

To verify the ER-derived cell surface estimates, cell membranes were stained with MemBrite 640/660 kit (Biotium) following cell adhesion to the 96 well plates. Fresh 1X dilutions of pre-staining buffer and dye solution were prepared in PBS from the 1000X stocks provided in the kit. 50 μL of 1X pre-staining buffer was added to each well and cells were incubated for 5 min at 37°C. The liquid was vacuumed from the plate and replaced with 50 μL 1X dye solution. Again, the cells were incubated at 37°C for 5 min. The dye was vacuumed from the plate and the cells were washed twice with PBS. Cells were incubated in 100 μL PBS for imaging.

Live yeast single time point imaging was performed on a Nikon W1 SoRa at room temperature using a 63× oil objective (NA = 1.49) with 4× magnification for a pixel size of 0.027 μm. Yeast cells were imaged in 3D (40–70 z sections, 0.2 μm apart). The GFPmut3 and mCherry fluorophores were excited with 488 nm and 561 nm illumination respectively. The MemBrite cell surface stain was excited at 640 nm. Theoretical resolutions for downstream sample analysis were calculated using the following equations:

For Axial Resolution: 0.4 λ/NA

For Lateral Resolution: 1.4 λ ⋅ η/NA2 (with η = 1.515 for the refractive index of oil).

Using the equations above, theoretical lateral resolution for the wavelengths (λ) 488nm and 561nm were calculated to be 131 nm and 151 nm respectively. Theoretical axial resolution for the wavelengths 488nm and 561nm were calculated to be 347 nm and 399 nm respectively. The volume cutoff of 0.009 μm3 used for filtering contacts was computed from the product of the squared theoretical lateral limit of resolution and the axial resolution for mCherry.

Single timepoint yeast images were denoised using Nikon Elements and then processed in MitoGraph to obtain 3D renderings. For each single cell, the ROI was copied across channels in order to keep the resulting renderings aligned. The cell surface was estimated using a Delaunay 3D filter on the rendering of the ER channel or on the rendering of the cell surface channel if the cell surface was marked with MemBrite.

To validate the use of MitoGraph, these same images were rendered using Imaris’ default background subtraction to detect surfaces. Surfaces were rendered individually for each fluorescent channel and then exported for further analysis in ParaView and Blender.

#### Timelapse

A single colony from a YPD plate containing yTK32 was inoculated into SC-Glu media and grown overnight in 24 well plates. The overnight culture was inoculated into 1 mL SC-Glu in 1:500, 1:1000, 1:2000 dilutions. These cultures were set to grow overnight at 30°C in 24 well plates at 200 RPM. Once the cells reached mid-exponential phase (OD600 = 4.5), cells were diluted 1:50 in SC-Glu in a fresh 24-well plate. Cells were then adhered to 96-well plates pretreated with concanavalin A. One hour prior to imaging, adhered cells were washed three times with 150 μL GE media, leaving at least 50 μL of media in the well each time to avoid cell stress. Yeast were then imaged in 200 μL of GE media.

Live yeast timelapse images were acquired on the Nikon AX NSPARC using an Apo TIRF 60× Oil objective (NA = 1.49) with a 5× magnification for a pixel size of 0.057 μm. Yeast cells were imaged in 3D (40–70 z sections, 0.17 μm apart). The GFPmut3 and mCherry fluorophores were excited with 488 nm and 561 nm illumination respectively.

Yeast timelapse images were deconvolved using Nikon Elements and then processed in MitoGraph to obtain 3D renderings. For each single cell, the ROI was copied across channels and timepoints in order to keep the resulting renderings aligned. The cell surface was estimated using a Delaunay 3D filter on the rendering of the ER channel.

#### Mammalian culture and imaging

24-48 h post transfection, the cells were washed with PBS and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, 0.05% glutaraldehyde in PBS. Samples were then permeabilized with ice-cold methanol for 20 min at −20°C then blocked for 20 min in PBS containing 0.01% Triton, 5% goat serum and 5% human serum. Cells were then ready for overnight primary staining with PTPIP51 (Sigma-Aldrich, HPA009975) diluted 1:750 in block or with Pex14 (Abcam, ab183885) diluted 1:500, for mitochondria and peroxisome imaging, respectively.

Following washes, Alexa Fluor 647 was diluted 1:2,000 in block and incubated with the cells for 1 h. Images were acquired on a Nikon W1-SoRa at 60x with a 2.8× SoRa magnification. 17-point Z-stacks were taken of every image with a Z-step of 0.19μm. Nikon Elements was used for denoising and deconvolution of images.

Mammalian images were rendered using Imaris’ background subtraction (local contrast) automatic settings. Automatic threshold values were used without adjustments.
